findings.reason: Untrusted source: rf_num_slots is a peer-controlled le16 count in a DLM_RCOM_STATUS_REPLY recovery message from a remote cluster node; receive_sync_reply (fs/dlm/rcom.c:263) memcpy's the peer h_length bytes into ls->ls_recover_buf, and dlm_process_incoming_buffer (fs/dlm/midcomms.c:81-105) validates only h_length (<= ci_buffer_size=4096) against the buffer, never the embedded slot count. Violated invariant: dlm_slots_copy_in checks only !num_slots; the sibling local-generation path dlm_slots_assign (fs/dlm/member.c:276-283) does enforce max_slots = (ci_buffer_size - sizeof(dlm_rcom) - sizeof(rcom_config)) / sizeof(rcom_slot) and rejects num_slots exceeding it, so the receive/peer direction is asymmetrically unvalidated (same mirror-path shape as the seed). Unsafe use: the first loop at member.c:124-127 performs in-place endian conversion writes at ro0[i] for i in [0,num_slots) - sizeof(struct rcom_slot)==16, so with num_slots up to 65535 the loop walks past the 4096-byte kmalloc'd ls_recover_buf (fs/dlm/lockspace.c:581) in both read and write; a second loop at member.c:132-141 then reads the same OOB entries (ro->ro_nodeid, ro->ro_slot) into memb->slot. Even when the happy path would be safe, every failure exit inside the loop (slot-changed, no-slot) returns without unpoisoning the already-endian-converted buffer or the consumed num_slots, and ls_generation has already been overwritten from the peer message. Impact: remote-triggerable OOB read+write of adjacent heap memory during DLM recovery by any node with cluster-network access (the DLM threat model: peer nodes are semi-trusted, but a compromised/malicious node or MITM on the unencrypted dlm socket reaches this path); the writes are endian-conversions (bswap32/16 of OOB data) so corruption is value-restricted but the read feeds memb->slot. Counterevidence checked: midcomms h_length bound is the only length gate; check_rcom_config (rcom.c) validates only lvblen/lsflags/version, not slot counts; DLM_MAX_SLOTS does not exist in this tree; a possible future guard would be max_slots-style clamp like member.c:276.
findings.conclusion: dlm_slots_copy_in loops on peer rf_num_slots (le16, up to 65535) with only a !num_slots check while sibling dlm_slots_assign clamps to max_slots - remote OOB read+bswap-write of 16-byte entries past the 4096-byte ls_recover_buf during DLM recovery.

findings.quote:
for (i = 0; i < le32_to_cpu(pplhdr->entries_count); i++) {
		struct ppl_header_entry *e = &pplhdr->entries[i];
findings.reason: Untrusted source: pplhdr->entries_count is a u32 read from the on-disk PPL header page (ppl_load_distributed reads PAGE_SIZE via sync_page_io at raid5-ppl.c:928-933 and gates only on page CRC and signature, not on the count). Violated invariant: the write path enforces io->entries_count == PPL_HDR_MAX_ENTRIES (raid5-ppl.c:274) before appending entries, but the recovery mirror path ppl_recover iterates le32_to_cpu(pplhdr->entries_count) with no clamp - asymmetric validation. Unsafe use: entries[] is a fixed PPL_HDR_MAX_ENTRIES (~126) array inside a single page (include/uapi/linux/raid/md_p.h:411-426); a crafted header with entries_count > 126 makes ppl_recover_entry index past the page, and each entry's pp_size (le32) also drives repeated sync_page_io disk reads. The error-unwind shape: any -EIO inside the loop jumps to out: freeing the page but the poisoned count has already driven OOB entry reads; CRC over the whole page is the only gate, so a local attacker with write access to the member disk (or a corrupted/malicious disk) controls the count while passing CRC. Counterevidence checked: the header CRC covers the full PAGE_SIZE including entries_count, but CRC is not a trust boundary against a disk attacker; requires mdadm-configured PPL, dirty array start (mddev->recovery_cp != MaxSector), and write access to the PPL region. This matches the prior sibling report (i052/f051 medium) and is independently confirmed in s13 at the recovery lines.
findings.conclusion: raid5-ppl ppl_recover iterates on-disk le32 entries_count with no PPL_HDR_MAX_ENTRIES clamp that write path raid5-ppl.c:274 enforces - crafted-but-CRC-valid PPL header walks entries[] past the header page during recovery (prior-audit lead confirmed in s13).

Beyond the intent's named leads, no systematic tree-wide sweep for other early-return paths leaving untrusted counts in shared objects (e.g. other fs/dlm receive handlers like receive_rcom_names, other md recovery readers) was completed before finalization.

drivers/scsi/elx/libefc_sli/sli4.c and drivers/net/ethernet/emulex/benet be_cmds.c firmware-response field conversions flagged as follow-ups by sibling facts f045/f049 (s11/s12) were not audited in s13 in this session.
The dlm finding's exploitability depends on DLM cluster peer trust assumptions (unencrypted lowcomms, no node authentication); the practical reachability from a non-member host was not verified.
limitations: dlm finding: the OOB writes are endian byte-swaps of out-of-bounds read data (ro_nodeid bswap32, ro_slot bswap16), restricting achievable corruption values, and the target ls_recover_buf is exactly ci_buffer_size (default 4096, sysfs-tunable) so the overflow distance and adjacent objects depend on the configured buffer size.

dlm finding: a peer must reach the DLM_RCOM_STATUS_REPLY receive path with matching rc_seq_reply (receive_sync_reply checks rc_id against ls_rcom_seq at rcom.c:250-263), so the attacker is a node that already participated in recovery sequencing - a compromised cluster member or on-path attacker, not an arbitrary host.

raid5-ppl finding requires local write access to the PPL region of an mdadm-managed member disk plus a dirty-array restart, and the header CRC must be recomputed after tampering; it is the same site sibling fact f051 already reported from s13 under branch2, listed here for the branch3 (error-unwind) angle only.

The finalize directive stopped the investigation early: candidate count reached is 8 classified plus 4 absence-confirmed leads; no compile/reproducer validation of the dlm OOB walk was performed (source-only analysis).
